routes.description: Establish that theism has a defensible prior and that fine-tuning, consciousness, ordered complexity, and observer existence jointly favor a limitless, knowledgeable, and morally perfect creator over relevant alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cumulative observations raise the probability of the specified being enough to warrant belief, with an adequate account of why the evidence points beyond an unspecified designer to the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being in the motion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative evidential comparison to rationally warranted belief in the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Establish a non-negligible prior for theism through simplicity, fundamentality, and the absence of arbitrary limits.
Show that observations can support theism through likelihood comparisons when assessed together with priors and cumulative evidence.
Show that life-permitting constants and complexity-generating laws are substantially more expected under purposive creation than under agentless alternatives.
Show that conscious lives and observer existence are more expected if a morally perfect, unconstrained creator has reason to create valuable lives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why observer selection, a single observed universe, or unknown alternative constants need not eliminate the evidential force attributed to fine-tuning.
Account for the universe's scale, hostility, development, and divine nonmanifestation insofar as they bear on its fit with purposive creation.

routes.description: Establish that the available observations do not discriminate the specified deity from natural, selection-based, or rival intentional explanations and therefore do not supply sufficient warrant for belief in an omnimax, morally perfect being.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative's likelihood claims lack adequate priors, comparison classes, causal discrimination, or an attribute-level bridge, or if features such as hiddenness and suffering materially undermine the prediction that this morally perfect being would produce the observed world.

motionBridge.description: Show that the evidence presented does not warrant belief in the all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being named by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Require evidence to discriminate the proposed deity from competing explanations rather than merely remain consistent with intentional creation.
Show that conditional likelihood alone does not identify the actual cause without defensible priors, alternatives, and background causal information.
Test whether observer selection, unknown parameter possibilities, and the single-universe setting block the inference from life-permitting conditions to design.
Require a justified transition from evidence for possible agency or power to maximal knowledge, maximal power, and moral perfection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether moral perfection and self-sufficiency actually predict the creation of conscious, imperfect beings.
Assess whether hiddenness, unreliable supernatural expectations, suffering, and cosmic hostility fit the proposed morally perfect creator.

sections.title: Evidential Standards and Bayesian Support
sections.rationale: This issue governs when comparative likelihood, prior probability, and cumulative observations count as evidence rather than mere compatibility, determining how every substantive argument connects to warranted belief.

sections.title: Theistic Prior and the Omnimax Attribute Bridge
sections.rationale: The motion concerns a specifically all-knowing, all-powerful, morally perfect being, so the case must address both the prior plausibility of theism and the transition from a possible designer to those maximal attributes.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Observer Selection
sections.rationale: Life-permitting constants and ordered complexity form the most sustained evidential clash, encompassing design analogies, comparison classes, possible parameter values, anthropic selection, and rival explanations.

sections.title: Consciousness, Observer Existence, and Divine Motivation
sections.rationale: The predicted existence of conscious people depends on both their comparative probability under alternative worldviews and whether a morally perfect, unconstrained being would have reason to create them.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness and the Observed World's Fit
sections.rationale: Hiddenness, suffering, cosmic hostility, and unreliable supernatural expectations bear directly on whether the observed world is expected under a morally perfect creator and therefore on the motion-level inference.

moves.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
moves.proposition: Hypotheses should be assessed by both their prior probability and how much more strongly the observed evidence is predicted by them than by alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the core likelihood claim for the heavily weighted fine-tuning section.

moves.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
moves.proposition: An observer's own existence favors theism if existence is likelier in worlds containing more possible people and an unlimited good God would create the maximal population.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops observer-population evidence and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring contact.

moves.proposition: Belief should track independently testable evidential support, with judgment reserved when a claim lacks sufficient rational warrant.

moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness and unreliable supernatural expectations count against belief in a morally perfect God who allegedly wants humans to know and relate to it.

components.text: Whether a morally perfect creator's alleged concern for conscious agents fits unclear and unreliable divine disclosure.
Whether moral perfection is supported by the observed epistemic arrangement.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Hiddenness supplies a relevant tension, but the sweeping comparative moral judgment is stronger than the developed premise.

charity.alternative: A perfect God may have reasons to permit epistemic distance or noncoercive relationship formation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such reasons must explain why rational inquiry often fails to yield clear, reliable awareness of the proposed God.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expectation-to-observation contrast is coherent, but the premise about desired disclosure and the comparative moral conclusion remain compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts rational evidence standards with apparent divine exemption and argues that rewarding unjustified faith conflicts with the proposed attributes.

moves.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
moves.proposition: A perfect unlimited mind predicts life and consciousness more parsimoniously than a merely powerful being whose capacities terminate at unexplained arbitrary limits.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Matthew's timed rebuttal and explicitly answers a question attributed to Matt about limited versus unlimited power.

components.text: Why the evidence should favor an unlimited perfect mind rather than a creator with bounded capacities.
Whether arbitrary limits make the bounded alternative less parsimonious despite verification limits.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly contacts the identification challenge but does not fully resolve verification or moral-perfection concerns.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative claim is clear, but arbitrary limit, defect, perfection, and simplicity retain partly unsettled meanings.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply supplies a real comparative consideration, but treats the parsimony advantage and divine motivations more confidently than supported.

charity.alternative: A bounded creator might be ontologically simpler than an unlimited perfect mind even if its exact limits require specification.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative must show that eliminating numerical limits offsets the added content of perfection, mentality, and creative motives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative reply is intelligible, but absence of limits does not by itself establish moral perfection or the claimed creative predictions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central contacts, it directly attacks the negative omnimax-identification bridge.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: An outcome being more probable under intentional arrangement does not by itself justify concluding that this particular outcome was intentionally produced.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly starts Matt's rebuttal, after which Matt gives a continuous first-person card, Galton-board, and dice argument.

components.text: Whether greater likelihood under intentional arrangement is sufficient to infer that the observed constants were intentionally selected.
Whether comparative predictive likelihood alone completes the causal inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly attacks the decisive transition from likelihood compatibility to causal identification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately claims insufficiency of the isolated likelihood fact, not impossibility of an intentional inference with additional evidence.

charity.alternative: A Bayesian design argument can use likelihood ratios together with priors and cumulative evidence rather than infer intention from probability alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example validly shows that greater probability under intention is not alone sufficient for actual-cause identification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central contacts, it directly establishes the negative inference-gap bridge.

moves.proposition: A primordial message in later human languages would differ categorically from fine-tuning because organisms adapt to existing physics rather than showing that they were its intended goal.
moves.attributionBasis: Matthew's question hands the floor to Matt, whose first-person answer distinguishes invented human languages from evolved life under physical conditions.

Whether life-permitting conditions demonstrate that existing life was the intended goal.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even if only one universe among many could sustain life, observing oneself in that universe would not establish that it was intentionally created.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt answers Matthew's direct question, reiterates his uncertainty about variable constants, and develops a continuous multiverse and observer-selection response.

components.text: Whether observing the sole life-permitting universe discriminates intentional creation from accidental generation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the decisive inference from observed viability to intention.

moves.proposition: Observer selection does not erase fine-tuning evidence, because an event required for one's observation can still favor intentional explanation when it is otherwise highly improbable.
moves.attributionBasis: Matthew explicitly turns to Matt's earlier observation objection and gives sustained parental and firing-squad analogies before returning to God.

moves.speaker: Matthew Adelstein
moves.proposition: Theism can become warranted when the explanatory force of several observations is combined cumulatively with its prior probability, even if no single observation suffices.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly identifies this reasoning as Adelstein's opening-statement framework and presents it in his first-person argumentative voice.

components.text: Whether multiple likelihood contributions combined with a prior can warrant belief despite each item's individual insufficiency.
